newsitem.title: INDIA: India party to hold poll amid leadership row.
newsitem.headline: India party to hold poll amid leadership row.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's party played down a crisis on Wednesday and went ahead with plans to elect a leader after failed efforts to bring around its angry chief, who threatened to split the group.

Party leaders said the Janata Dal, which heads the ruling United Front coalition, was scheduled to hold its presidential election on Thursday despite a call by president Laloo Prasad Yadav's supporters to boycott the poll.

Former prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda denied rumours he was scheduled to meet Yadav, a popular low-caste leader and chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, who is at the centre of a political corruption scandal which has engulfed the party.
"There is no option other than elections. This is an attempt to create confusion in the minds of voters," Deve Gowda told reporters.
The upheaval in Gujral's party has shaken the ruling 15-party alliance barely two months after he assumed power following a month-long political crisis.
"There will be no compromise. No one can stop the election," Sharad Yadav, who is contesting against Laloo Prasad Yadav, told Reuters.
The Janata Dal is facing trouble on two fronts involving Laloo Yadav.
One is a $280 million animal welfare scandal, and the other the party poll in which Laloo Yadav has alleged that the voters' list has been manipulated to favour his rivals.
Party officials deny the charge. "I will not allow anybody
to capture the party by proxy and that is why I have given a call for boycott of the elections," Yadav told Reuters in Patna, Bihar's capital.

The United News of India said Laloo Yadav's supporters were planning to hold a "parallel" convention in Patna on Saturday to elect a new leader. If that takes place, it could signal a split in the Janata Dal.

A party leader, who asked not to be named, said Gujral himself was in trouble after his decision on Monday to transfer the federal police chief, Joginder Singh, who was investigating the "fodder" scandal in which Laloo Yadav has been indicted.
"They have put a snake around Gujral's neck," the leader said.
Opposition parties and leftist allies accused the government of political motives in replacing Singh as director of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI).

The government said the transfer would not hamper investigations into the scandal involving the alleged siphoning off of animal welfare funds. Laloo Yadav is one of 56 officials and politicians accused by the CBI.
Yadav has denied any wrongdoing in the case and refused to resign as state chief minister and face trial. This is widely regarded as having hurt the party's image.

Yadav's strong base in Bihar is a key concern for party leaders, who have to choose between the desire to have a clean image and the popular vote base of Laloo Yadav, who commands a sizeable following among low castes and minority Moslem voters.
